title: Codimension One Foliations and Secondary Classes

items.title: Divisibility by a nowhere-vanishing one-form
items.statement: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\omega$ be a nowhere-vanishing smooth $1$-form on $M$. (i) If $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$ satisfies $\alpha\wedge\omega=0$, then there is a unique $f\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\alpha=f\omega$. (ii) If $\theta\in\Omega^2(M)$ satisfies $\theta\wedge\omega=0$, then there is $\beta\in\Omega^1(M)$ with $\theta=\beta\wedge\omega$.
items.strategy: Pointwise linear algebra in a local coframe $(\omega,\theta_2,\dots,\theta_n)$: writing $\alpha=f\omega+\sum_{i\ge2}a_i\theta_i$ and expanding $\alpha\wedge\omega$ in the basis $\{\theta_i\wedge\omega\}$ forces $a_i=0$, so $\alpha=f\omega$ locally, and $f$ is determined because $\omega$ is nowhere vanishing; the local functions agree on overlaps, giving (i) globally. For (ii), in the same coframe the coefficients of $\theta_a\wedge\theta_b\wedge\omega$ in $\theta\wedge\omega$ are the coefficients of the $\theta_a\wedge\theta_b$ part of $\theta$, so $\theta=\beta\wedge\omega$ locally with $\beta=\sum_i b_i\theta_i$. On overlaps the difference $\beta_U-\beta_V$ satisfies $(\beta_U-\beta_V)\wedge\omega=0$, hence is $f\omega$ by (i); patching with a partition of unity gives a global $\beta$ because the corrections vanish under $\wedge\,\omega$. Both assertions are local computations; no choice principle is used.

items.title: Restriction of a foliation transverse to the boundary
items.statement: Let $W$ be a smooth $(n+1)$-manifold with boundary and let $F$ be a codimension-one regular foliation of $W$ transverse to $\partial W$, i.e. $T_p(\partial W)+T_pF=T_pW$ for every $p\in\partial W$. Let $\omega$ be a nowhere-vanishing smooth defining $1$-form for $F$. Then: (i) $T_p(\partial W)\cap T_pF$ has dimension $n-1$ for every $p\in\partial W$, and these subspaces form a codimension-one regular foliation $F|_{\partial W}$ of the smooth $n$-manifold $\partial W$; (ii) the restriction $\omega|_{\partial W}$ is nowhere vanishing and defines $F|_{\partial W}$, with $\omega|_{\partial W}\wedge d(\omega|_{\partial W})=0$; (iii) every leaf of $F|_{\partial W}$ is a connected component of $L\cap\partial W$ for a leaf $L$ of $F$; (iv) if $F$ is transversely oriented by $\omega$, then $F|_{\partial W}$ is transversely oriented by $\omega|_{\partial W}$; (v) if $\eta$ is a $1$-form on $W$ with $d\omega=\eta\wedge\omega$, then the pullback of $\eta$ to $\partial W$ satisfies $d(\omega|_{\partial W})=(\eta|_{\partial W})\wedge(\omega|_{\partial W})$.
items.strategy: Work in a boundary slice chart in which $\partial W$ is a coordinate hyperplane. Transversality says exactly that $\omega|_{\partial W}$ is nowhere vanishing on $T\partial W$, so $\ker(\omega|_{\partial W})=T\partial W\cap\ker\omega$ is a hyperplane field on $\partial W$; the dimension count gives (i) and (ii). Integrability is inherited by pulling back $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ along the inclusion using [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-commutes-with-pullback]] and [[prop-pullback-of-forms-is-smooth-functorial-and-preserves-wedges]], then applying [[cor-codimension-one-frobenius-criterion]]. Leaves are maximal connected integral manifolds, so connected components of $L\cap\partial W$ are maximal integral manifolds of the restricted distribution, giving (iii); the transverse orientation restricts by construction, and (v) is the pullback of the defining identity. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The Bott partial connection on the normal bundle of a foliation
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a codimension-$q$ regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$, with tangent distribution $E=TF$, and let $
u:=TM/E$ be the normal bundle of $F$ ([[def-quotient-vector-bundle-by-a-subbundle]]). For a leaf-tangent vector field $X\in\Gamma(E)$ and a section $s\in\Gamma(
u)$ the **Bott partial connection** is $
abla^{B}_X s:=\pi\,[X,	ilde s]$, where $	ilde s\in\Gamma(TM)$ is any smooth representative of $s$ and $\pi:TM	o
u$ is the quotient map. This defines a map $
abla^{B}:\Gamma(E)	imes\Gamma(
u)	o\Gamma(
u)$ that is $C^\infty(M)$-linear in the vector-field variable $X$, $\mathbb R$-linear in $s$, and satisfies the Leibniz rule $

The quotient bundle and its quotient map are the published constructions cited. The connection is only defined along leaf directions, which is exactly what is needed for the curvature computation of lem-curvature-of-an-extending-bott-connection-lies-in-the-transverse-differential-ideal.

items.title: The winding number jumps by one across a regular planar arc
items.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be an oriented closed piecewise-$C^1$ contour. Suppose that near $0$ it contains exactly one regular $C^1$ arc, traversed once with positive real tangent, and that the remaining contour is a compact set disjoint from $0$. Then for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $i\varepsilon$ and $-i\varepsilon$ avoid $\Gamma$ and $n(\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$.
items.strategy: The real coordinate of the arc has derivative $1$ at $0$. Shrink its parameter interval so this derivative remains positive; the mean value theorem makes the coordinate strictly increasing and the intermediate value theorem gives an interval as its image. Its inverse is $C^1$ by the difference quotient and the positive derivative bound. Thus the arc is a graph, and after shrinking write it as $z(x)=x+if(x)$ for $-a\le x\le a$, with $f(0)=f\prime(0)=0$ and $|z\prime(x)|\le2$. Choose $\eta<1/2$ and shrink $a$ so $|f(x)|\le\eta|x|$. The remaining parameter pieces form a compact set disjoint from $0$. For each parameter in them, continuity gives a relative interval on which $|z|$ exceeds half its positive value at that parameter; all such intervals have a finite subcover by compactness, and the minimum of the finite positive bounds is some $d>0$. For $\varepsilon<d/2$ both test points avoid the remainder; they also avoid the local graph because its real coordinate vanishes only at $x=0$, where $z(0)=0$. By the winding definition, linearity, and oriented reparametrization, the index difference is $(2\pi i)^{-1}$ times the integral of $2i\varepsilon/(z^2+\varepsilon^2)$ along $\Gamma$. On the remainder, the denominator factors $|z-i\varepsilon||z+i\varepsilon|$ are at least $d^2/4$, so the ML estimate bounds that contribution by a constant times $\varepsilon$. On the local graph, $|z(x)-i\varepsilon||z(x)+i\varepsilon|\ge c(x^2+\varepsilon^2)$ for one $c>0$: for $|x|\ge\varepsilon$ use $|z(x)\pm i\varepsilon|\ge|x|$, and for $|x|<\varepsilon$ use $|f(x)|\le\eta\varepsilon$. With $x=\varepsilon u$, the local integral becomes $\int_{-a/\varepsilon}^{a/\varepsilon}2i z\prime(\varepsilon u)/((z(\varepsilon u)/\varepsilon)^2+1)\,du$. Its integrand converges uniformly on every bounded $u$-interval to $2i/(1+u^2)$ and is bounded in modulus by $C/(1+u^2)$; hence the tails are uniformly $O(1/R)$ outside $[-R,R]$. The limit is $2\pi i$, since the integral on $[-R,R]$ is $4i\arctan R$. Therefore the index difference tends to $1$. Each index is an integer by [[thm-winding-number-is-integer]], so the difference equals $1$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. The proof uses only the stated winding/line-integral facts, finite local estimates, and no general Jordan theorem or choice axiom.

items.title: The winding number is locally constant by an integral estimate
items.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a closed rectifiable contour of length $L$ and let $p_0$ lie off its trace. If $d>0$ satisfies $|z-p_0|\ge d$ for all $z\in\Gamma^*$ and $|p-p_0|<d/2$, then $\left|n(\Gamma,p)-n(\Gamma,p_0)\right|\le L|p-p_0|/(\pi d^2)$. In particular the winding number is locally constant on the complement of the trace.
items.strategy: Subtract the two defining integrals and use $1/(z-p)-1/(z-p_0)=(p-p_0)/((z-p)(z-p_0))$. Since $|p-p_0|<d/2$, each point of the contour has $|z-p|\ge d/2$ and $|z-p_0|\ge d$, so the integrand difference has modulus at most $2|p-p_0|/d^2$. The ML estimate and the factor $(2\pi i)^{-1}$ give the displayed bound. For any fixed $p_0$ off the contour trace and each parameter $t$, continuity gives some relative interval $J$ around $t$ on which $|\Gamma(s)-p_0|>|\Gamma(t)-p_0|/2$. Take the family of all such pairs $(t,J)$; it covers the compact parameter interval, so finitely many pairs cover it. The minimum of their finitely many positive bounds is a suitable $d>0$, without choosing intervals simultaneously for all parameters. If $L>0$, shrink $|p-p_0|$ further so the bound is less than $1$; the difference of the two indices is an integer by [[thm-winding-number-is-integer]], hence is zero. If $L=0$, the ML estimate makes the defining contour integral zero for every point off the trace. Thus the index is locally constant. No general Jordan theorem or choice axiom is used.

items.title: C² local inverses and scalar return roots
items.statement: Let f be a C² map between open subsets of R^n with invertible derivative at a point. Its local inverse is C². If g(s,t) is C² near (s0,t0), g(s0,t0)=0 and g_t(s0,t0)≠0, then there is a unique local C² root t=T(s), with $T′=-g_s/g_t$ and $T″=-(g_{ss}+2g_{st}T′+g_{tt}(T′)^2)/g_t$, evaluated at (s,T(s)). No choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Use only the proved local-inverse clause of [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]. Its proof constructs the inverse by the deterministic Newton iteration from the specified initial point; the closed-ball completeness step uses only claim 2 (closed subspace of a complete space is complete in ZF) of [[thm-complete-subspace-iff-closed]], not its countable-choice converse. The derivative identity makes the C¹ inverse C² because matrix inversion is the adjugate/determinant formula on the open set of invertible matrices. Apply this to $(s,t)\mapsto(s,g(s,t))$ and restrict its inverse to $(s,0)$; differentiating $g(s,T(s))=0$ twice gives the displayed derivatives. Thus the invoked inverse/root clauses use no choice axiom; no smooth implicit-function theorem or stronger dependency clause is used.

items.title: A C¹ planar field on a closed disk extends C¹ to a neighborhood
items.statement: Let X be a planar vector field C¹ up to the boundary of the closed unit disk D. It has a C¹ extension to an open neighborhood of D whose value and first derivative agree with X on D, including its boundary. This is a finite explicit extension, with no choice axiom.
items.strategy: Use Cartesian vector components. For q=(1+s)p with p∈S¹ and 0<s<ε<1/2, set E(q)=3X((1−s)p)−2X((1−2s)p), and use E=X on D. On the boundary the coefficients sum to one. The tangential derivatives likewise have factor 3−2=1; the outward radial derivative has factor −3+4=1. Continuity of the up-to-boundary first derivatives therefore makes E and DE match X and DX across S¹. Each side is C¹, so the extension is C¹ on |q|<1+ε. For a parameter disk obtained by a fixed smooth coordinate change use the same formula on its pulled-back Cartesian components. No foliation or map extension outside D is asserted or needed.

items.title: A C² saddle function has C¹ Morse coordinates
items.statement: Let $f$ be C² near $p\in\mathbb R^2$, with $df(p)=0$ and Hessian of signature $(1,1)$. There is a C¹ local diffeomorphism $(x,y)$ centered at $p$ for which $f-f(p)=xy$. The coordinate change is only asserted to be C¹.
items.strategy:
Translate $p$ to the origin. Since the Hessian is indefinite, choose $v$ with positive quadratic value and an independent vector $e$; replace $e$ by $w=e-H(e,v)H(v,v)^{-1}v$. The Gram determinant is negative, so $H(w,w)<0$. In the resulting finite linear coordinates $f_{xx}(0)>0$, $f_{yy}(0)<0$, and $f_{xy}(0)=0$. Shrink until $f_{xx}>0$. By the local C¹ inverse theorem [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] applied to $(x,y)\mapsto(f_x(x,y),y)$, the equation $f_x=0$ is $x=\eta(y)$ for a C¹ function. Put $b(y)=f(\eta(y),y)$. Since $b'(y)=f_y(\eta(y),y)$ and $f_y$ is C¹, $b$ is C²; moreover $b''(0)=f_{yy}(0)-f_{xy}(0)^2/f_{xx}(0)<0$.

For $x\ne\eta(y)$ define $X(x,y)=\operatorname{sgn}(x-\eta(y))\sqrt{f(x,y)-b(y)}$, and set $X=0$ on the curve $x=\eta(y)$. Positivity under the square root follows from $f_{xx}>0$. Off that curve, $2XX_x=f_x$ and $2XX_y=f_y-b'(y)$. The mean-value formula and continuity of the Hessian give the limits along the curve
$X_x=\sqrt{f_{xx}/2}$ and $X_y=f_{xy}/\sqrt{2f_{xx}}$, evaluated at $(\eta(y),y)$. These are also the derivatives of the defined X on the curve: the first follows from the second-order expansion in $x-\eta(y)$, and the second from $\eta'=-f_{xy}/f_{xx}$. The displayed limits are continuous, so X is C¹ across the curve and $X_x(0,0)>0$.

Likewise define $Y(y)=\operatorname{sgn}(y)\sqrt{b(0)-b(y)}$ and $Y(0)=0$. Since $b''(0)<0$, the one-variable mean-value formulas show Y is C¹ near zero with $Y'(0)=\sqrt{-b''(0)/2}>0$. Thus $(x,y)\mapsto(X,Y)$ is a C¹ local diffeomorphism by the C¹ inverse theorem, and $f-f(0)=X^2-Y^2$. The linear change $(X,Y)\mapsto(X+Y,X-Y)$ gives coordinates with product $(X+Y)(X-Y)=f-f(0)$. All choices are finite; only the stated C¹ inverse, explicit two-dimensional orthogonalization and mean-value clauses are used. The inverse step invokes only the choice-free local-inverse proof: deterministic Newton iteration and the ZF closed-subspace direction of completeness, never its countable-choice converse.

items.title: Taut codimension-one foliations
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a codimension-one regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$, transversely oriented in this pair. $F$ is **taut** if for every leaf $L$ of $F$ there is a closed transversal through $L$: an embedded smooth loop $\gamma:S^1\to M$, everywhere transverse to $F$, with $\gamma(S^1)\cap L\neq\varnothing$. On a compact connected $M$ the leaf-by-leaf condition is equivalent to the existence of a single closed transversal meeting every leaf (lem-a-taut-foliation-of-a-compact-connected-manifold-is-met-by-a-single-closed-transversal), and the form-theoretic criterion is prop-a-leafwise-positive-closed-two-form-calibrates-a-taut-foliation.
items.strategy: The definition records the leaf-by-leaf form used in the sources; the single-transversal and closed-form forms are proved as separate items so that each use declares the form it needs. Transversality of loops uses [[def-map-transverse-to-a-regular-foliation]]. The three forms (leaf-by-leaf, single loop, closed $2$-form nondegenerate on leaves) are equivalent in the cited sources and are kept separate on this page.

items.title: Dead-end components
items.statement: Let $F$ be a transversely oriented codimension-one foliation of a smooth manifold $M$. A **dead-end component** of $F$ is a compact embedded submanifold with boundary $N\subsetneq M$, saturated for $F$ (a union of leaves, so that its boundary is a union of leaves), such that the co-orientation of $F$ points inwards along every component of $\partial N$: every transverse curve starting in $N$ in the positive direction remains in $N$. A transversely oriented foliation with no dead-end component is called **dead-end free**. This is the compact form of the notion; the open formulation (an open saturated set admitting no properly immersed transverse line) describes the interior of a dead-end component in other treatments.
items.strategy: The definition uses the submanifold-with-boundary and saturation vocabulary; 'the boundary is tangent to $F$' says exactly that $\partial N$ is a finite union of leaves, and compactness makes the trapping condition topological: a transverse curve entering $N$ cannot leave without ceasing to be transverse. The co-orientation sign is part of the definition because it is exactly the hypothesis used in the volume-form and closed-form criteria of this page.

items.title: The accessible manifold of a leaf
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a transversely oriented codimension-one foliation of $M$ and $L$ a leaf. The **accessible manifold** $N_L$ of $L$ is the set of points $p\in M$ for which there is a smooth curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, transverse to $F$, with $\gamma(0)\in L$ and $\gamma(1)=p$, parametrised so that it crosses leaves in the positive direction. Equivalently, $N_L$ is the union of the leaves reachable from $L$ by positive transverse curves. It is open and saturated, and $F$ is taut if and only if $N_L=M$ for every leaf $L$.
items.strategy: The set is well defined because transversality is open on compact parameter intervals, so small perturbations do not destroy it, and $N_L$ is a union of leaves: once a transverse curve reaches a point of a leaf, its endpoint can be moved within the leaf along plaques. The leaf-by-leaf form of tautness says exactly that every leaf lies in the positive reach of every other leaf, i.e. $N_L=M$ for every $L$; this is Goodman's accessible-manifold criterion, used in lem-a-foliation-is-taut-if-and-only-if-it-has-no-dead-end-component.

items.title: The Bott partial connection is well defined and flat along leaves
items.statement:
In the notation of [[def-bott-partial-connection-on-the-normal-bundle-of-a-foliation]], the Bott partial connection is well defined: $\pi[X,	ilde s]$ depends only on $X\in\Gamma(E)$ and the section $s\in\Gamma(
u)$, not on the representative $	ilde s$, is $C^\infty(M)$-linear in $X$, and satisfies $
abla^B_X(fs)=X(f)s+f
abla^B_X s$ for $f\in C^\infty(M)$. Its curvature vanishes along leaves: for all $X,Y\in\Gamma(E)$ and $s\in\Gamma(
u)$, $R^B(X,Y)s:=
abla^B_X
abla^B_Y s-
abla^B_Y
abla^B_X s-
abla^B_{[X,Y]}s=0$.
items.strategy: If $\tilde s'=\tilde s+\sigma$ with $\sigma\in\Gamma(E)$, then $[X,\tilde s']=[X,\tilde s]+[X,\sigma]$ and $[X,\sigma]\in\Gamma(E)$ because $E$ is involutive, so $\pi[X,\cdot]$ is well defined. Linearity in $X$ and the Leibniz rule follow from $[fX,\tilde s]=f[X,\tilde s]-(\tilde s f)X$ with $(\tilde s f)X\in\Gamma(E)$ and from $[X,f\tilde s]=X(f)\tilde s+f[X,\tilde s]$. For flatness, compute in $TM$ using the Jacobi identity: the lifted expression $[X,[Y,\tilde s]]-[Y,[X,\tilde s]]-[[X,Y],\tilde s]$ is zero, and all terms are well defined modulo $E$; projecting gives $R^B=0$. This is Bott's verification (1), (2) and the Jacobi computation of the 'basic connection'; no choice principle is used.

items.title: A C² leaf meets a local box transversal in at most countably many points
items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a $C^2$ foliation on a second-countable smooth manifold, let $L$ be a leaf, and let $\tau:J\to Q$ be a vertical transverse interval in one foliation box. Then $\tau^{-1}(L)$ is at most countable. If a countable foliation-box atlas is supplied as part of the data, the countability conclusion uses no choice principle. Dense and nonembedded leaves are allowed.
items.strategy: Use [[thm-second-countable-implies-lindelof]] and the stated ACω to obtain a fixed countable foliation-box atlas, with the selected charts recorded as cover data. A C² atlas is in particular the plaque-preserving C¹ atlas of [[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]]. Start at one plaque through a fixed point of L. In plaque coordinates, the intersection of a reached plaque with a next box is open; its components are open and connected by [[cor-components-of-open-subsets-of-rn-are-polygonally-connected]]. Code each nonempty component by the least rational-box basis index contained in it. Each (next-box index,component code) determines at most one successor plaque, since the new transverse coordinate is locally constant and thus constant on that connected component. Every plaque in L is reached by a finite chain. Encode the finite sequence of integer pairs by [[def-natural-number-coding-of-finite-sequences]], and assign each reached plaque in Q its least valid code. This injects those plaques into the natural numbers without a countable union of countable families or a selection at every plaque. Each such plaque meets the vertical transversal at most once. Therefore τ^{-1}(L) injects into the natural numbers. The only countable choice was extraction of the atlas; no embedded-leaf topology or full AC is used.

items.title: A finitely cornered regular plane curve separates without choice
items.statement: Let $c:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$ be a piecewise-$C^2$ topological embedding with finitely many corner parameters. Assume each smooth edge is regular up to its endpoints and the two incident one-sided tangent rays at each corner are distinct. Then $\mathbb R^2\setminus c(S^1)$ has exactly two connected components, one bounded and one unbounded, and each has boundary $c(S^1)$. No choice axiom is assumed.
items.strategy: Orient the curve by its parameter. The circle $S^1$ is compact by Heine–Borel, and any open cover of $c(S^1)$ pulls back to an open cover of $S^1$; hence $c(S^1)$ is compact and closed. Because $c$ is an embedding, every sufficiently short open parameter arc has image open in $c(S^1)$ and therefore equals $c(S^1)\cap O$ for some ambient open set $O$. At a smooth edge point choose linear coordinates with tangent horizontal. The first coordinate has nonzero derivative along the parametrized edge; after shrinking, its derivative has fixed sign, so the mean value theorem makes it strictly monotone and the intermediate value theorem shows its image is an interval. The inverse is $C^1$ by the difference quotient and derivative lower bound, giving a local graph. At a corner choose a linear coordinate whose derivative has opposite signs on the two distinct outward tangent rays and apply the same one-sided argument to both incident branches; they join to one local graph. Choose an ambient rectangle inside $O$ in which this graph is the entire curve portion. Its complement in the rectangle has exactly two connected sides, which the orientation labels left and right. These parameter arcs cover $S^1$; compactness yields a finite subcover. The overlap graph of this finite cover is connected, since otherwise the unions of parameter arcs in two graph components would separate the connected circle. Whenever two parameter arcs overlap, their rectangles overlap near a common curve point, and the left-side patches (respectively right-side patches) meet there: both are the same oriented side of the same local graph. Thus the unions $V_+$ and $V_-$ of all left and right patches are connected subsets of the complement, and every curve point is approached from each. At a smooth edge point $p$ with unit tangent $\tau$, use the oriented coordinate $w=\bar\tau(z-p)$. The defining integral is unchanged because $dw/(w-w_0)=dz/(z-z_0)$ when $w_0=\bar\tau(z_0-p)$. The local winding-jump lemma in these coordinates gives different indices on the two side unions near $p$. The local integral-estimate lemma makes the index constant on each connected component, so $V_+$ and $V_-$ lie in distinct components. Now let $U$ be any component of the open complement. By [[thm-components-partition-and-are-closed]] it is closed relative to the complement, and by [[cor-components-of-open-subsets-of-rn-are-polygonally-connected]] it is open in the plane. Its boundary is contained in the curve. This boundary is nonempty: otherwise $U$ would be a nonempty proper clopen subset of the connected plane, contradicting [[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]]. At a boundary point, the local graph patch has exactly two connected sides; $U$ meets one side, so that entire side belongs to $U$ and identifies $U$ with one of the two global collar-side components. Thus there are at most two components, while $V_+$ and $V_-$ show there are at least two. Their local sides approach every curve point, so the curve is the boundary of both; conversely no component boundary lies off the curve. Finally [[thm-complement-of-a-compact-plane-set-has-one-unbounded-component]] makes exactly one component unbounded, and the other is bounded. All choices in the collar construction are finite; neither Jordan–Brouwer nor Jordan–Schönflies nor full AC is used.

items.title: C¹ Euclidean maximal flows, variational dependence and the finite C² upgrade
items.statement: Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹ diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies $W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.
items.strategy:
On a fixed compact convex cylinder, the componentwise mean-value bound makes Y Lipschitz with one constant L and bounds |Y| by M. Choose one h with hM below the state margin and hL<1. The bounded-cylinder clause of [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] supplies the common local family; its Picard iteration starts at the specified constant curve and is deterministic. The quantitative [[thm-continuous-dependence-of-odes-on-initial-data-and-parameters]] estimate gives uniform C⁰ dependence. These uses concern compact Euclidean cylinders, not a general metric compactness equivalence.

For an initial increment u, subtract the Volterra equations. Put $A_u(t)=\int_0^1 DY(\Phi(t,p)+r(\Phi(t,p+u)-\Phi(t,p)))\,dr$. Uniform C⁰ dependence and uniform continuity of DY on the cylinder give A_u→DY(Φ(t,p)) uniformly. The variational matrix integral equation V=I+∫DY(Φ)V has a unique solution on every fixed compact time interval: local Picard for the linear equation, the Grönwall exponential bound, and the finite-endpoint Cauchy continuation argument below extend it there. Subtracting V(t)u from the solution difference and applying [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]] gives an error o(|u|), uniformly in t. Hence D_pΦ=V. The same integral estimate at nearby p gives continuity of V; ∂tΦ=Y(Φ) is continuous, so Φ is jointly C¹.

For Y∈C², the coefficient C(t,p)=DY(Φ(t,p)) is C¹ in p, with derivative D²Y(Φ)D_pΦ. Difference quotients of V solve inhomogeneous linear integral equations; the same uniform-continuity/Grönwall remainder argument converges to W′=CW+D²Y(Φ)[Ve_i,Ve_j], W(0)=0, and proves W continuous in (t,p). Thus D²_pΦ exists continuously. The mixed derivative is DY(Φ)D_pΦ and the second time derivative is DY(Φ)Y(Φ), giving joint C² without a smooth-only dependence theorem. For Y∈C¹, a trajectory is C² in time by differentiating x′=Y(x) once.

Uniqueness glues all local solutions into maximal ones and proves the flow law; no solution is chosen from an arbitrary family. On a compact solution segment finitely many common local cylinders and composition prove openness of D and C¹ regularity (C² for C² Y). Flow-law inversion gives the inverse slice Φ_{−t}. At Y(q)≠0 choose a fixed linear transversal σ and apply the C¹ inverse-function theorem to (t,z)↦Φ(t,σ(z)); for C² Y use [[lem-c2-inverses-and-scalar-return-roots]] for its C² inverse. If a trajectory stays in compact K⊂⊂U and a maximal endpoint were finite, bounded Y gives |x(t)−x(s)|≤M|t−s|, so its finite endpoint limit exists by Euclidean completeness, lies in K, and local Picard extends it. This avoids a subsequence/metric-equivalence/DC route. The linear variational equations use the same bounded-derivative Cauchy endpoint argument. The exact direct Picard, Grönwall, Euclidean compactness and inverse clauses require no full AC; unrelated full-AC/DC mentions in broad supplier metadata are not invoked.

Choice-use register for the clauses actually invoked: the Picard iterates start at the named constant curve and are generated by ordinary recursion; the inverse-flow/flow-box step uses only the local C¹ inverse conclusion of [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]], whose deterministic Newton proof uses the ZF closed-subspace direction (claim 2) of [[thm-complete-subspace-iff-closed]]. The maximum and uniform-continuity facts are applied to the specified compact coordinate cylinders in their finite-subcover forms, not through sequential-compactness equivalences. No DC or full AC clause is invoked; broad unused dependency metadata does not enter this proof.

items.title: Positive transverse accessibility between leaves
items.statement: Let F be a C² transversely oriented codimension-one foliation on a smooth manifold M without boundary, with its chosen positive transverse direction. A positive transverse segment is a C² map c:[0,1]→M whose transverse derivative is strictly positive in every positively signed foliated chart, including the one-sided endpoint derivatives. It is an immersed curve and need not be embedded. For leaves A,B write $A\succeq_F B$ when A=B or when such a nonempty segment has c(0)∈A and c(1)∈B. The clause A=B is formal reflexivity, corresponding to Novikov’s empty-segment convention; it does not assert a positive return segment or a closed transversal. This is the direction of Novikov’s A≥B: the positive segment goes from A to B.
items.strategy: Use the plaque/leaf and signed transverse chart vocabulary of [[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]] at C² regularity. Positive chart changes have positive transverse derivative, so the sign condition is independent of the chart. The binary relation is defined by the displayed existential clause together with formal reflexivity. Its transitivity and endpoint-independence for a genuine nonempty segment are established in [[lem-positive-transverse-accessibility-is-a-preorder]]. No actual segment is inferred from the equality clause.

items.statement: For an oriented C² surface, every compact subset lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated subsurface. Finite oriented polygon reduction supplies closed genus normal forms, free groups for nonempty-boundary subsurfaces, torsion-free fundamental groups, and an embedded disk bounded by every embedded null curve, unique unless the entire surface is a sphere. These clauses use at most ACω.
items.title: Finite surface normal forms, Jordan disks, and torsion control
items.strategy:
For a compact set K choose finitely many relatively compact surface charts covering it and finitely many C² coordinate bump functions whose sum f exceeds1 on K and has compact support. Sard for the C² scalar f gives a regular a∈(0,1). The union of the components of {f≥a} meeting K is a compact subsurface S with C² boundary and K in its interior; it has finitely many components because its compact regular boundary and compact manifold chart cover give finite component charts. In a noncompact connected surface, a connected component containing connected K has nonempty boundary: an empty-boundary compact codimension-zero region would be open and closed and equal the whole surface.

Construct a finite cellulation of S without using arbitrary Jordan curves. Choose finitely many coordinate disks with smaller cores covering S. Move their radii generically so their boundary circles and ∂S intersect transversely, with no triple points; the C² scalar Sard clause on each of the finitely many prior arcs supplies these radii. Add all finitely many crossings as graph vertices. Each arrangement face has constant membership in every disk, hence lies in one disk whose core-cover point it contains. Within that coordinate disk, straighten finite regular arcs near their vertices and replace each compact regular edge by a close polygonal edge inside its disjoint thin strip. Compact inverse-function neighborhoods ensure the replacement is a graph over the old edge, so stripwise interpolation is an ambient isotopy. For an isolated closed regular curve, its short normal collar is injective by compactness and IFT; a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon is a graph in that collar and isotopic to it. Thus only the choice-free polygonal Jordan theorem is required. Add finite planar crosscuts between distinct boundary components of an arrangement face, then triangulate its simple polygonal faces by ears. Reconcile the finite subdivisions on shared edges. Reversing the strip isotopies gives a finite curvilinear triangular cellulation of S. This is the finite supplied-chart part of the published curvilinear construction, with its full-AC arbitrary-Jordan input replaced by the regular-curve polygon argument just given.

Cut a spanning tree of the finite primal graph and a spanning tree of the dual graph to obtain one finite polygon schema (published one-polygon lemma, proof steps1.1–3.1). All orientable paired sides occur with opposite traversal signs. The finite schema moves cancel adjacent aa^{-1}; an interlaced pair a,b is cut and pasted into one handle block aba^{-1}b^{-1}, which is set aside. If no pair interlaces, an innermost adjacent inverse pair exists and cancels. Each operation deletes a pair or sets aside a block, so finite side count decreases. Unpaired boundary circles remain boundary circles. The result is genus g with b boundary circles, χ=2−2g−b; for b>0, the standard polygon edge retraction gives the free group on 2g+b−1 generators. These are the finite operations in the published polygonal reduction-moves item, not its full-AC triangulation-existence premise. For b=0 the same schema gives sphere for g=0, torus for g=1, and the usual oriented genus-g model; χ=0 identifies exactly the torus. Finite regular chart and collar smoothing makes the model maps C² diffeomorphisms in the present C² category.

Torsion-freeness is local to a compact subsurface: a loop and a null cap of its m-th power have compact connected image K, so lie in such an S. With boundary, π₁(S) is free and cyclic reduction of a nonempty reduced word shows its positive powers stay nonempty. For closed S, genus0 has trivial group and genus1 has Z². For genus≥2 split off one handle: van Kampen writes the group as an amalgam of two free groups over the infinite cyclic boundary subgroup. The boundary word is a nonempty cyclically reduced product of commutators in each free factor, so those edge injections are injective. The published amalgam normal-form theorem then makes any finite-order element conjugate into a factor: an alternating cyclically reduced word has powers of strictly increasing syllable length. Thus no torsion exists. Its coset data require no full AC here: free groups have explicit finite-word enumerations, and one chooses the first word in each cyclic coset.

Finally take an embedded null curve c and its compact null cap, include them in S and cellulate with c as a subgraph by the same finite regular arrangement. If c is nonseparating, a crossing dual curve gives algebraic intersection1, so c is not null. If it separates and neither side is a disk, their boundary subgroup generated by c injects in each side: the finite polygon word is nonempty in each non-disk oriented boundary surface. Van Kampen and amalgam normal form would then make c nontrivial in S, contradicting the supplied null cap. Hence one side is a disk, embedded in S and therefore in the original surface. If both sides are disks their union is an open-and-closed sphere surface; otherwise the disk is unique. The same argument applies to a simply connected leaf cover without identifying it globally with the plane.

items.title: Frobenius divisibility: d omega equals eta wedge omega
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a transversely oriented codimension-one foliation of a smooth manifold $M$ with nowhere-vanishing defining $1$-form $\omega$, so $TF=\ker\omega$. Then $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ and there exists a smooth $1$-form $\eta$ on $M$ with $d\omega=\eta\wedge\omega$. If $\eta'$ is another such form, then $\eta'-\eta=f\omega$ for a unique $f\in C^\infty(M)$.
items.strategy: Since $F$ is integrable, [[cor-codimension-one-frobenius-criterion]] gives $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$, equivalently $d\omega\wedge\omega=0$ by [[thm-wedge-product-is-associative-and-graded-commutative]]. Apply [[lem-forms-annihilated-by-a-nowhere-vanishing-one-form-are-divisible-by-it]] (ii) to $\theta=d\omega$: there is a global $1$-form $\eta$ with $d\omega=\eta\wedge\omega$. If $d\omega=\eta'\wedge\omega$ as well, then $(\eta'-\eta)\wedge\omega=0$, and part (i) of the same lemma gives $\eta'-\eta=f\omega$ with $f=\eta'(X)-\eta(X)$ for any vector field $X$ with $\omega(X)=1$; this also shows $f$ is unique. No choice principle beyond the standing vocabulary is used.

items.title: Smooth foliated concordance of codimension-one foliations
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold and let $F_0,F_1$ be transversely oriented codimension-one foliations of $M$ with defining forms $\omega_0,\omega_1$. A **smooth foliated concordance** from $F_0$ to $F_1$ is a codimension-one regular foliation $G$ of $W:=M\times[0,1]$, transverse to the two boundary slices $M\times\{0\}$ and $M\times\{1\}$, together with a nowhere-vanishing defining $1$-form $\omega$ for $G$ such that for $j=0,1$ the pullback $i_j^{*}\omega$ along $i_j(x):=(x,j)$ is a defining form for $F_j$. By [[lem-a-foliation-transverse-to-the-boundary-restricts-to-the-boundary]] each slice $M\times\{j\}$ carries the codimension-one foliation $G|_{M\times\{j\}}$ with defining form $i_j^{*}\omega$, so the requirement is exactly that these boundary foliations be $F_j$ with the prescribed co-orientations.
items.strategy: The product $M\times[0,1]$ is a smooth manifold with boundary and its slices inherit smooth structures; transversality of $G$ to the slices is the standard relation, so the restriction lemma applies and produces the boundary foliations. The definition records the classical product-type foliated concordance used for secondary-class invariance. The concordance, foliations, and defining forms are smooth, and the boundary coorientations are matched. No orientation of $M$ is required.

items.title: A taut foliation of a compact connected manifold has a single closed transversal
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a taut codimension-one foliation of a compact connected smooth manifold $M$. Then there is a single closed transversal $\gamma$ meeting every leaf of $F$.
items.strategy: Every closed transversal meets an open saturated union of leaves: transversality is open, and in a product chart a transversal meets all plaques near a point, so the set of leaves met is open in the leaf space. By compactness of $M$, finitely many closed transversals $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n$ meet every leaf; choose such a family with $n$ minimal and let $M_i$ be the open saturated set of leaves met by $\gamma_i$. If $M_i\cap M_j\neq\varnothing$, choose a leaf $\lambda$ meeting both and an embedded path $\sigma\subset\lambda$ joining the two intersection points; the loop $\gamma_i*\sigma*\gamma_j*\sigma^{-1}$ is monotone, and perturbing it in product charts along the leafwise segments turns it into a closed transversal meeting every leaf of $M_i\cup M_j$, contradicting minimality. Hence the $M_i$ are disjoint open saturated sets covering the connected $M$, so $n=1$. This is Calegari's Lemma 4.26 and Ranz's equivalence of conditions (i), (ii), (iii); only the standing countable choice is used.

items.title: Curvature of an extending Bott connection lies in the transverse differential ideal
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a codimension-$q$ regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$ with normal bundle $
u=TM/TF$, let $
abla^{B}$ be the Bott partial connection, and let $
abla$ be any connection on $
u$ extending it: $
abla_X=
abla^B_X$ for every $X\in\Gamma(TF)$. Let $I\subseteq\Omega^*(M)$ be the differential ideal generated by the $1$-forms that vanish on $TF$, i.e. the ideal locally generated by a coframe of the annihilator bundle of $TF$. Then, in a local frame of $
u$ that is parallel along the leaves for $
abla^B$, the curvature matrix entries of $
abla$ lie in $I$; consequently every coefficient of the curvature two-form $R^
abla\in\Omega^2(M;\mathrm{End}\,
u)$ lies in $I$, and $I^{q+1}=0$.
items.strategy:
An extension exists because the space of connections on a vector bundle is an affine space modelled on $\Omega^1(M;\mathrm{End}\,
u)$ and the difference of two connections is an endomorphism-valued $1$-form; patching the partial connection with an arbitrary connection over a foliated-chart cover with a partition of unity produces a global connection extending $
abla^B$. On a foliated chart, choose a local frame of $
u$ parallel along the plaques for the flat partial connection $
abla^B$ (solve the linear ODE along the simply connected plaques using $R^B=0$). In that frame the connection $1$-forms $	heta^a_b$ of $
abla$ satisfy $	heta^a_b(X)=0$ for $X\in\Gamma(TF)$, so $	heta^a_b\in I$. The structure equation $R=d	heta+	heta\wedge	heta$ then gives $R^a_b=d	heta^a_b+\sum_c	heta^a_c\wedge	heta^c_b$; both terms lie in $I$ because $d$ of a form vanishing on $TF\wedge TF$ (equivalently an element of $I$) again vanishes on $TF\wedge TF$, and products of elements of $I$ lie in $I$. Finally $I^{q+1}=0$: the ideal is generated by $q$ one-forms that are pointwise linearly independent, and a product of $q+1$ of them is zero because some generator is repeated and $	heta\wedge	heta=0$. This is Bott's Lemma (6.4) and the paragraph preceding it; Cite DG-38's Chern-Weil comparison ([[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]]) for the interpretation of the curvature matrix. No choice principle beyond the standing countable choice is used.

items.title: Relative generic position for characteristic disk maps
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a $C^2$ cooriented codimension-one foliation of a smooth $3$-manifold, and let $h:D^2\to M$ be a $C^2$ disk map. Suppose its boundary is either a smooth loop in one leaf or a closed transversal. In the leaf-boundary case, $h$ is homotopic relative to $\partial D^2$ to a map with a fixed collar on which the pulled-back characteristic covector is nonzero; in the transversal-boundary case a smaller collar of $h$ already has this property. Keeping that regular collar fixed, one can homotope the map relative to the boundary so that all characteristic singularities are interior, finite, and nondegenerate. Each singularity is a center or saddle. The statement does not assert that distinct singular points map into distinct ambient leaves.
items.strategy: A transverse boundary already has a regular collar by continuity. For a leaf-boundary loop, cover the compact boundary circle by finitely many source intervals whose small half-collars map into foliation boxes. Subdivide once more to choose compact cores still covering the circle. In each box add a small chartwise perturbation to the transverse coordinate that vanishes on the boundary and has strictly positive inward radial derivative on its core; use a bump supported in the corresponding half-collar. Chart changes reparameterize the transverse coordinate by a local diffeomorphism, so nonvanishing of its differential is invariant. Perform this finite sequence in order, choosing each perturbation small enough in $C^1$ to preserve the nonzero covector already obtained on earlier compact cores. The map remains fixed on the boundary, and the resulting covector is nonzero on the full boundary; compactness then supplies a smaller regular collar. This uses only finitely many chart choices and no ambient geodesic interpolation. On the compact remainder choose finitely many domain coordinate patches $V_i$ with compact cores $K_i$ covering it, such that the current disk map sends each $\overline V_i$ into one target foliation chart $Q_i$ with positive margin. Reserve a small $C^2$ neighborhood preserving these chart inclusions. In chart coordinates write the current map as $(Y_i,u_i)$, where $u_i$ is the local transverse coordinate. Choose a compactly supported bump $\rho_i$ in $V_i$, equal to $1$ near $K_i$, using [[lem-manifold-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]. For a small vector $a\in\mathbb R^2$, replace the map on $V_i$ by $\chi_i^{-1}(Y_i,u_i+\rho_i(a\cdot x))$ and leave it unchanged outside; because the bump vanishes on a neighborhood of $\partial V_i$, this is an actual $C^2$ map glued with all derivatives and fixed on the boundary collar. On the neighborhood where $\rho_i=1$, its critical points satisfy $\nabla u_i(x)=-a$. The gradient map is $C^1$; [[thm-morse-sard-for-euclidean-maps]] at $m=n=2,r=1$ makes its critical values null, and the critical values have empty interior. Indeed, if a Euclidean null set contained a ball, choose a closed nondegenerate square $Q$ inside it. Let $Q$ be a closed square of side $L\le1$ contained in the ball, and choose by nullity a sequence of closed covering cubes $C_n$ with side lengths $\ell_n$ and total area at most $L^2/4$. Since these cubes are closed, first thicken them: for $n\ge1$ set $\delta_n=\min(1,L^2/(128\cdot2^n(\ell_n+1)))$ and let $C_n^+$ be the open cube with the same center and side $\ell_n+2\delta_n$. Since $\ell_n^2\le L^2/4$ and $L\le1$, we have $\ell_n\le L/2\le1/2$. Expanding the square gives $4\ell_n\delta_n+4\delta_n^2\le L^2/(96\cdot2^n)+L^2/(4096\cdot2^n)<L^2/(64\cdot2^n)$. Thus the total added area is less than $L^2/64$, and the open cubes still cover $Q$ with total area less than $17L^2/64<L^2/2$. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], compactness gives a finite subcover with total area $V_f<L^2/2$. Apply [[lem-finite-cube-covers-admit-grid-control]] to this finite cover of $Q$, with $\eta=L^2/2$: its grid cells are all of $Q$, so $L^2<V_f+L^2/2<L^2$, a contradiction. The compactness step uses [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. Thus arbitrarily small regular values exist without any choice principle. At each such point $D^2u_i$ is invertible, so the local transverse function has a nondegenerate critical point. The zero-transversality condition on a compact core is open: around each existing Morse zero keep its Hessian invertible, and on the remaining compact set keep the gradient bounded away from zero. Thus each later chart perturbation can be chosen small enough to preserve all earlier cores. The finite cover yields a final map with only nondegenerate interior critical points; these are isolated and finite by compactness and the regular collar. Chart changes have the form $u' = φ(u)$ with $φ'\ne0$, so they preserve the critical set, nondegeneracy and center/saddle type. At a definite Hessian, Taylor expansion gives a strict radial derivative on a small punctured disk; every sufficiently close level meets each ray once, and the implicit-function theorem makes the radii continuous, giving closed level circles (a center). At an indefinite Hessian, linearly choose $u_{xx}(0)>0$, $u_{yy}(0)<0$. The inverse-function theorem [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] solves $u_x=0$ as $x=\eta(y)$. Put $b(y)=u(\eta(y),y)$; then $b\in C^2$, $b(0)-b(y)=y^2B(y)$ with continuous $B>0$, and Taylor integration in $x$ gives $u(x,y)-b(y)=(x-\eta(y))^2A(x,y)$ with continuous $A>0$. The local changes $X=\operatorname{sign}(x-\eta(y))\sqrt{u(x,y)-b(y)}$ and $Y=\operatorname{sign}(y)\sqrt{b(0)-b(y)}$ are monotone local coordinates, so $u-u(0)=X^2-Y^2$; the four-sector level picture is a saddle. This proves the $C^2$ singularity classification without invoking a smooth Morse lemma. Scaling each finite perturbation parameter gives a homotopy fixed on the boundary. This is a map-level scalar perturbation; it neither assumes nor proves an immersion approximation, a distinct-leaf condition for the tangencies, or elimination of saddle connections.

items.title: A C² product coordinate on a planar period annulus
items.statement: Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$. Let $A$ be an open annulus saturated by $X$, with $X$ nowhere zero on $A$, such that every orbit in $A$ is a simple periodic curve and these curves are strictly nested Jordan curves with a consistent orientation. Then there are an interval $I=(0,1)$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\Psi:S^1\times I\to A$ taking each circle $S^1\times\{s\}$ onto one orbit and a positive $C^2$ function $a:I\to(0,\infty)$ such that $X=a(s)\partial_\theta$ in these coordinates. The coordinate may be chosen to increase from the inner end to the outer end of the annulus.
items.strategy:
Let $J$ be the standard quarter-turn in the plane and choose the sign of $Z=\pm JX$ so this nonzero $C^2$ transverse field points from the bounded Jordan domain of each orbit toward its exterior. This sign is consistent on $A$, since the orbit curves are nested and their orientation is consistent. Start the unique maximal $Z$-trajectory $\sigma$ at one specified point of one orbit. It crosses each orbit at most once: every crossing has the same inward-to-outward direction, so a second crossing of the same Jordan curve would require a crossing in the reverse direction. It meets every orbit between its two endpoint leaves. Indeed, nested Jordan separation forces it to cross every intermediate orbit; if the range of crossed leaves had an endpoint that was still in $A$, a flow box around that compact regular orbit would give a uniform nonzero transverse speed and extend the crossing past the endpoint. Thus the $Z$-trajectory is a global section and its flow parameter ranges over an open interval.

For each section point $\sigma(s)$, the $X$-orbit is periodic with a least positive period $T(s)$. The section $\sigma$ is $C^2$ by that same finite-grade flow clause for $Z$, and the local flow of the $C^2$ field $X$ is jointly $C^2$ by the explicit second-variation clause of [[lem-c1-euclidean-maximal-flow-with-c2-upgrade]]. Hence the scalar return equation $g(s,t)=0$ in a flow-box coordinate is $C^2$ and has a strictly nonzero derivative in the time variable at the reference return. The one-variable mean-value and difference-quotient argument first gives $T\in C^1$ locally and $T\prime(s)=-g_s/g_t$ for the local return equation $g(s,T(s))=0$, whose time derivative $g_t$ is nonzero. Differentiating this identity once more gives $T\prime\prime(s)=-(g_{ss}+2g_{st}T\prime+g_{tt}(T\prime)^2)/g_t$, so $T\in C^2$. Compactness of one reference orbit prevents an earlier return from appearing under a small change of $s$. Reparameterize the section interval by an increasing $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto $(0,1)$, and set $\Psi(\theta,s)=\Phi^X_{\theta T(s)}(\sigma(s))$. The two coordinate derivatives are independent because one is tangent to $X$ and the other is transverse. The map is bijective since the section meets every orbit once and time modulo the least period parametrizes each orbit once. For a local inverse near a point, flow a nearby point back by the fixed reference time and solve $r(\Phi_{-u}^X(q))=0$ for the unique small time $u$ by the same scalar-root argument; this root is $C^2$ in $q$. The intersection point on the graph section has a $C^2$ section parameter by its one-dimensional graph inverse, and the elapsed time divided by $T(s)>0$ gives the phase. Thus $\Psi$ has local $C^2$ inverses, which agree globally by bijectivity, proving it is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism. Finally $\partial_\theta\Psi=T(s)X$, so $a(s)=1/T(s)>0$. Only the specified initial section point and finite local compactness arguments are used; no circle-bundle classification or countable choice is invoked. The return root and local inverse are exactly the C² clauses of [[lem-c2-inverses-and-scalar-return-roots]]. This standalone result retains X∈C² and its constant-speed a(s); it is not used for the merely C¹ characteristic generator.

items.title: Local generalized Poincaré–Bendixson theorem for a precompact planar orbit
items.statement: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $Y:U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^1$ vector field. Let $\mathcal O^+(y)=\{Y_t(y):t\ge0\}$ be a positive orbit whose closure $K_0=\overline{\mathcal O^+(y)}$ is compact and satisfies $K_0\Subset U$. Put $K=\omega^+(y)=\bigcap_{T\ge0}\overline{\{Y_t(y):t\ge T\}}$, and assume $K$ contains only finitely many equilibria. Then exactly one of the following forms holds: (i) $K$ is a singleton equilibrium; (ii) $K$ is one regular periodic orbit; (iii) $K$ is a nonempty finite set $E$ of equilibria together with at least one regular trajectory, and every regular point of $K$ lies on such a trajectory whose alpha- and omega-limit sets are points of $E$. The family of connecting trajectories in (iii) need not be finite.
items.strategy:
Use $K=\bigcap_{T\ge0}\overline{\{Y_t(y):t\ge T\}}$. The tail closures are nested nonempty compact connected sets, so the finite-intersection property makes $K$ nonempty, compact and connected; flow continuity and the flow law make it invariant. These claims use compactness of the given orbit closure, not a sequential compactness theorem.

At a regular point choose a compact transverse interval $\Sigma$ inside a flow box. A finite cover of $\Sigma$ by smaller flow boxes gives a positive lower bound on the time between distinct consecutive crossings accumulating on $\Sigma$, so crossings cannot accumulate at finite time. If the orbit is not periodic, its consecutive intersections with $\Sigma$ are distinct. The intervening orbit arc and the section subarc between two consecutive intersections form an embedded piecewise-$C^2$ closed curve with two transverse corners: uniqueness prevents self-intersections, and consecutiveness excludes another section hit on the arc. Apply [[lem-finitely-cornered-regular-plane-curve-separates-without-choice]]. The vector field crosses the section consistently and cannot cross the orbit arc by uniqueness. If the first two crossing coordinates satisfy $p_1>p_0$ in the chosen section coordinate, the Jordan side containing the forward orbit at the second corner meets the section beyond $p_1$, so the next crossing satisfies $p_2>p_1$; if $p_1<p_0$, the same argument gives $p_2<p_1$. Repeating this argument makes all consecutive crossing coordinates strictly monotone in that same direction. A repeated crossing instead makes the orbit periodic by uniqueness. Any point of $K\cap\Sigma$ is a limit of crossings of the original orbit: in a flow box, late orbit points near that point move to $\Sigma$ by a uniformly bounded signed time. Monotonicity therefore implies $K\cap\Sigma$ has at most one point.

For a regular $z\in K$, each one-sided limit set of its orbit is nonempty, compact, connected and contained in $K$, by the same nested-tail argument. If such a limit set contained a regular point, the corresponding semiorbit would cross a section infinitely late. The crossing bound just proved forces all those crossings to be the unique point of $K$ on that section; a repeated crossing makes $z$ periodic. If $K$ also contains an equilibrium, this is impossible: a finite flow-box tube around that periodic orbit meets $K$ only in the orbit, because any nearby point of $K$ flows to a second point on the transverse interval. The orbit is therefore both open and closed in $K$, contradicting connectedness unless it is all of $K$. Thus, when equilibria occur, each one-sided limit set of every regular orbit is a connected subset of the finite equilibrium set and hence a singleton. If no equilibrium occurs, a regular point of $K$ has a nonempty one-sided limit set containing a regular point, so the same argument makes its orbit periodic; the one-point section bound and connectedness give $K$ equal to that periodic orbit. If there are no regular points, connectedness makes $K$ a single equilibrium. This proves exactly the three alternatives. The proof reproduces the finite-equilibrium content of Teschl, Theorem 7.16, but makes no assertion that alternative (iii) has finitely many connecting trajectories. All local flows, inverse flow boxes and finite-time continuity use the C¹ clause of [[lem-c1-euclidean-maximal-flow-with-c2-upgrade]]. Each time-parametrized orbit of a C¹ field is C², so the finite-corner Jordan separator applies to the orbit arcs and a straight transverse interval; C² dependence on the initial point is not required.

items.title: A C1 hyperbolic planar gradient has local stable and unstable curves
items.statement: Let u be C² near a nondegenerate saddle in the Euclidean plane. Its C¹ field −∇u has local C¹ stable and unstable embedded curves tangent to the positive and negative Hessian eigenlines. Each curve has two half-trajectories, and every trajectory staying sufficiently near the saddle for all forward (respectively backward) time is on the stable (respectively unstable) curve. The corresponding convergence is exponential.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems; complete author-hosted text
references.locator: §9.2, Theorems 9.3–9.5, printed pp.255–259; the following local symmetric two-dimensional proof includes the C1 parameter argument

items.strategy:
Translate the saddle to zero. The real symmetric invertible matrix A=−Hess(u)(0) has one negative and one positive eigenvalue; the quadratic characteristic formula gives orthogonal eigenlines and projections P_s,P_u. Choose λ>0 below their absolute eigenvalues. Write X(x)=Ax+R(x), with R C¹ and R(0)=DR(0)=0. Multiply R by an explicit smooth radial cutoff supported in a small ball. The cutoff derivative contributes O(sup|R|/radius)=o(1), so its global Lipschitz constant ε is arbitrarily small. For 0<β<λ and stable coordinate a define T_a on continuous paths with norm sup_{t≥0}e^{βt}|z(t)| by T_a z(t)=e^{tA}a+∫_0^t e^{(t-r)A}P_s R(z(r))dr−∫_t^∞ e^{(t-r)A}P_u R(z(r))dr. Direct exponential integration bounds its Lipschitz constant by ε((λ−β)^{-1}+(λ+β)^{-1})<1. Iterate from e^{tA}a; successive differences form a geometric bound, hence converge uniformly in the weighted norm to a unique continuous fixed point. Completeness here follows directly by taking pointwise limits and the uniform Cauchy bound; no general infinite-dimensional choice theorem is used. The fixed point solves the C¹ ODE by the continuous primitive and variation of constants, stays in the uncut ball for small a, and decays exponentially. Its initial value is a+h(a) with h valued in the unstable line.

The C¹ cutoff derivative is uniformly continuous on its compact support. Taylor remainders therefore satisfy |R(z+w)−R(z)−DR(z)w|≤ω(||w||∞)|w| with ω(δ)→0, uniformly for all path values. After exponential integration the same estimate holds in the weighted norm. Thus T_a is C¹ as a function of path and a; its path derivative has norm <1. The difference of two fixed points is bounded by |δa|/(1−k). Subtract the linearized fixed-point equation and use that uniform Taylor remainder to obtain differentiability, with derivative given by the convergent Neumann series ∑_{n≥0}(D_zT_a)^n D_aT_a. Uniform continuity of DR and the contraction bound give continuity of this derivative. At a=0, DR(0)=0, so Dh(0)=0. The graph is the desired C¹ embedded curve.

Conversely a bounded forward trajectory staying in the uncut ball obeys the same integral equation: variation of constants gives its stable part, while multiplication of the unstable part by e^{−tA} and boundedness give the terminal cancellation integral. Take ε also small enough that this operator is a contraction in the unweighted bounded-path norm. Its unique bounded fixed point is the already constructed weighted one. Therefore every such orbit lies on the graph; time reversal gives the unstable graph. In dimension one each punctured graph component is one trajectory: X is nonzero there, the C¹ coordinate component has one sign, and integrating its reciprocal joins any two points before the equilibrium. Its two signs lie in opposite negative-potential sectors by tangency to the negative Hessian eigenline. This supplies precisely the two Euclidean-gradient half-rays used in the cancellation scalar.

items.statement: For a compact C² oriented region W in a closed oriented smooth three-manifold, with oriented C¹ plane bundle E tangent to every boundary component and one common inward transverse direction, the finite sum of boundary Euler characteristics is zero. For a finitely cellulated compact oriented surface, a tangent section with isolated nondegenerate zeros has total index V−E+F.
items.title: Finite tangent index count and inward boundary sum
items.strategy:
First prove the finite surface index clause. The finite cellulation gives a handle layout consisting of one small disk for each vertex, one rectangular band for each edge, and one filling disk for each face. Build a tangent section with one radial source (+1) in each vertex disk, one linear saddle (−1) in each edge band, and one radial sink (+1) in each face disk. Match its nonzero directions on the product collars of adjacent handles; finite bump interpolation between vectors in a common open half-plane introduces no zero. Thus its index sum is V−E+F. To compare any other tangent section with finitely many nondegenerate zeros, join them by a section homotopy and perturb it generically relative its two ends. Its zero set in the surface×[0,1] is an oriented compact1-manifold, so the two end index sums agree by finite interval boundary cancellation. Genericity is obtained with finitely many frame bumps whose parameter derivatives span each fiber; Sard applies to the parameter projection, whose source dimension exceeds target dimension by1 and whose regularity is C². At the ends the local zero orientation is the sign of the invertible derivative, the usual index. Small smoothing/perturbation preserves these isolated indices.

For the three-dimensional boundary sum, avoid requiring a finite CW decomposition of W or a general Thom class. Choose one smooth transverse field V near W. Smoothly approximate a C¹ cooriented annihilator for E using finite coordinate convolutions and bumps, obtaining a smooth1-form ω′ with ω′(V)>0. Its kernel E′ is a smooth oriented rank2 subbundle. Projection along V gives an oriented C¹ bundle isomorphism E→E′. Choose a generic smooth section s of E′ near W, using finitely many local frame bumps spanning each fiber on compact W. The universal section map is a submersion in these finite parameters. Sard for the interior projection (smooth) and for its C² boundary restriction (dimension excess1) gives parameters for which s is transverse to0 on W and on ∂W. Its zero set is consequently a compact oriented1-manifold with boundary, and the signed sum of its boundary points is0. No countable or uncountable family of frame selections is used after the finite cover.

Pull its boundary restriction back through E→E′ to a tangent section on each boundary surface. This is C¹ and has isolated nondegenerate zeros; its indices equal those of the E′ section because the bundle isomorphism preserves orientation. If a C² homotopy is needed for the comparison above, approximate in the smooth E′ bundle on the C² boundary using finitely many chart convolutions; sufficiently small C¹ approximation preserves the nondegenerate zeros and indices. The finite surface clause identifies each component’s index sum with its finite χ=V−E+F. The ambient and plane orientations together orient the zero curves. Since the chosen transverse V points inward on EVERY boundary component, their induced boundary sign is the same negative of the tangent-section index on each component. Thus 0=−Σ_C χ(C). This is the needed finite tangent-Euler boundary-sum calculation established directly by zero curves, without assuming a full-AC Thom theorem or an unproved e_fin comparison. The finite cell counts equal homological χ by the published finite-CW Euler–Poincare theorem.

Regularity is interpreted in a fixed bundle, not by assuming that the tangent bundle of a C² surface has C² transition matrices. For the surface index comparison use its C² finite-polygon normal form to a smooth genus model. Transport a given tangent section by the derivative of this normal form; it is C¹. A finite C¹-small smooth approximation on that fixed smooth model preserves each nondegenerate zero and its determinant sign, and introduces none on the compact regular complement. Compare there with the explicit smooth handle section by a smooth finite-parameter section homotopy. Its oriented one-dimensional zero set gives the stated count. For the ambient boundary sum the restriction of the smooth ambient bundle E′ to the C² boundary is a C² bundle. Compare sections in E′, or transport their indices to the preceding smooth surface model through the oriented C¹ projection. Thus the required Sard excess-one maps are genuinely C²; no C² regularity of tangent transition derivatives is presumed.

items.title: The Godbillon-Vey form eta wedge d eta is closed
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a transversely oriented codimension-one foliation with defining form $\omega$ and $d\omega=\eta\wedge\omega$. Then $d\eta\wedge\omega=0$; the $2$-form $d\eta$ is divisible by $\omega$, i.e. $d\eta=\zeta\wedge\omega$ for a smooth $1$-form $\zeta$; $d\eta\wedge d\eta=0$; and $d(\eta\wedge d\eta)=0$. Consequently $\eta\wedge d\eta$ is a closed $3$-form on $M$.
items.strategy: Differentiate $d\omega=\eta\wedge\omega$, using $d^2=0$ and $\eta\wedge\eta=0$: $0=d\eta\wedge\omega-\eta\wedge d\omega=d\eta\wedge\omega-\eta\wedge\eta\wedge\omega=d\eta\wedge\omega$. By [[lem-forms-annihilated-by-a-nowhere-vanishing-one-form-are-divisible-by-it]] (ii) applied to $d\eta$ there is a global $\zeta$ with $d\eta=\zeta\wedge\omega$. Then $d\eta\wedge d\eta=(\zeta\wedge\omega)\wedge(\zeta\wedge\omega)=-\zeta\wedge\zeta\wedge\omega\wedge\omega=0$ by graded commutativity and $\omega\wedge\omega=0$. Finally $d(\eta\wedge d\eta)=d\eta\wedge d\eta-\eta\wedge d(d\eta)=0$ by the graded Leibniz rule and $d^2=0$. No choice principle is used.

items.title: Reeb components of a codimension-one foliation
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a codimension-one regular foliation of a $3$-manifold $M$, and let $X=\overline D^2\times S^1$ be the closed solid torus with its standard **Reeb foliation** $F_{\mathrm{Reeb}}$ ([[prop-reeb-foliation-of-the-solid-torus-has-the-boundary-as-a-leaf]]): the boundary $\partial X$ is a compact leaf diffeomorphic to $T^2$ and every interior leaf is a plane accumulating on $\partial X$. A **Reeb component** of $F$ is a saturated subset $R\subseteq M$, compact as a subset, for which there is a homeomorphism $\Phi:X\to R$ mapping leaves of $F_{\mathrm{Reeb}}$ onto leaves of $F|_R$ and $\partial X$ onto a leaf of $F$; equivalently, $R$ is compact and saturated, homeomorphic to the solid torus, has a single compact leaf as boundary, and its interior foliation is foliated-homeomorphic to the Reeb foliation. In the smooth models of this page the conjugacy may be taken smooth; in the general closed-leaf construction of lem-the-compact-leaf-produced-by-a-vanishing-cycle-bounds-a-reeb-component the source produces a foliated homeomorphism, so the topological form of the definition is the one used. A foliation with no Reeb component is called **Reebless**.
items.strategy: The standard Reeb foliation of the solid torus, its boundary leaf and its plane leaves are supplied by the cited proposition; the definition names the saturation type of that model inside an ambient foliation. Foliated homeomorphism rather than foliated diffeomorphism is used because Novikov's closed leaf bounds a component foliated homeomorphically by the Reeb model, possibly with a wilder rate of convergence of the plane leaves to the boundary leaf. Transverse orientability is part of the standing hypotheses of the page.

items.title: Bott vanishing for real Pontryagin monomials of a foliation
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a codimension-$q$ regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$ with normal bundle $
u=TM/TF$. Then every real Pontryagin monomial of total cohomological degree greater than $2q$ in the normal bundle vanishes: for every invariant polynomial $\varphi$ on the structure group of $
u$ of degree $k>q$, the characteristic class $\varphi(
u)\in H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(M;\mathbb R)$ obtained from the Pontryagin classes of $
u$ by [[def-pontryagin-classes-by-complexification]] is zero. No integral statement is made: the vanishing is of the real Chern-Weil form, hence of the real class.
items.strategy:
Choose a connection $
abla$ on $
u$ extending the Bott partial connection. By [[lem-curvature-of-an-extending-bott-connection-lies-in-the-transverse-differential-ideal]], in a leaf-parallel frame the curvature matrix entries lie in the ideal $I$ generated by the annihilator of $TF$, and $I^{q+1}=0$. An invariant polynomial $\varphi$ of degree $k$ evaluated on the curvature is a sum of products of $k$ matrix entries, hence lies in $I^k$; for $k>q$ we have $I^k\subseteq I^{q+1}=0$, so the Chern-Weil form $\varphi(R^
abla)$ is identically zero. By [[thm-chern-weil-homomorphism-is-independent-of-connection-and-natural]] the Chern-Weil class is independent of the connection and by [[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]] it agrees with the real characteristic class of $
u$, so that class vanishes. This is Bott's vanishing theorem (Bott, (6.4) and Theorem (7.10)); it is a real statement, with no integral refinement. No choice principle beyond the standing countable choice is used.

items.title: C² plaque transport and finite transverse fences preserve C² regularity
items.statement: Let a codimension-one foliation on a smooth manifold be given by a $C^2$ foliated atlas, meaning the charts and their inverses have two continuous derivatives and their transverse coordinate changes depend only on the transverse coordinate. Every finite plaque transport between $C^2$ local transversals is a $C^2$ local diffeomorphism germ. A finite family of $C^2$ trace maps agreeing on open overlap collars glues to a $C^2$ trace map. If its parameter derivative has nonzero transverse component in each piece, the glued trace remains transverse, including its one-sided derivatives at parameter endpoints. Holonomy and its homotopy invariance are supplied by the underlying $C^1$ atlas. These statements assert regularity of specified compatible pieces, not existence of a polycycle fence or an extremal cycle.
items.strategy: A $C^2$ atlas is a $C^1$ atlas in [[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]], so [[lem-c1-holonomy-is-a-well-defined-representation-into-transverse-germs]] supplies well-definedness and homotopy invariance. In one foliated chart, the transverse coordinate restricted to a transverse $C^2$ curve has nonzero derivative. Its local inverse is $C^1$ by [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]; differentiating the inverse formula $Dg=(Df\circ g)^{-1}$ once more shows $Dg$ is $C^1$, hence $g$ is $C^2$. Plaque transport keeps the transverse coordinate fixed and uses these restrictions/inverses, so finite composition is $C^2$. Compatible traces coincide as maps on open collars, so their derivatives through order two coincide there; this is the local definition of a $C^2$ glued map. Transversality is the same nonzero transverse component in either chart and survives the gluing. Extend the domain slightly on each side when checking an endpoint, or use the stated one-sided derivative. Everything is finite and choice-free once the atlas, transversals and compatible pieces are given.

items.title: The characteristic disk has one more center than saddle
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a cooriented codimension-one foliation of a smooth $3$-manifold and $h:D^2\to M$ a disk map in the relative generic position of [[lem-characteristic-disk-map-can-be-put-in-generic-position-rel-boundary]]. If its boundary is either contained in one leaf or is a closed transversal, then the characteristic line field has finitely many nondegenerate centers and saddles and their counts satisfy $c-s=1$. In particular there is at least one center.
items.strategy:
Write the global defining form as $\omega$ and in the standard oriented source coordinates put $\beta=h^*\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$. The relative-genericity supplier gives a nonzero boundary covector and finitely many nondegenerate interior zeros; the only compactness input in the following finite constructions is [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], whose proof is choice-free. Define $X$ by $\iota_X(dx\wedge dy)=\beta$, so $X=(Q,-P)$ and its normalized degree is the same as that of $(P,Q)$, since this is a fixed orientation-preserving quarter-turn.

First compute the degree on $\partial D^2$. If $h(\partial D^2)$ lies in one leaf, then $\beta(\tau)=0$ for its positive tangent $\tau$. Since $\beta$ is nonzero there, $X$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $\tau$ with constant sign; thus its degree is $1$. If the boundary is a closed transversal, $\beta(\tau)$ is nowhere zero and has constant sign. Write $X=a n+b\tau$, with $n$ the outward normal. From $\beta(\tau)=(dx\wedge dy)(X,\tau)=a(dx\wedge dy)(n,\tau)$ and $(dx\wedge dy)(n,\tau)>0$, $a$ has fixed nonzero sign. The straight homotopy from $X$ to $n$ when $a>0$, or to $-n$ when $a<0$, never vanishes. Both $n$ and $-n$ wind once, so the boundary degree is again $1$.

Let $p_1,\dots,p_N$ be the zeros. Finiteness and their interior location give a zero-free annular collar of $\partial D^2$. Choose a regular polygon centered at the origin, sufficiently close to the circle that its boundary lies in this collar and it contains all $p_i$; let $Q_0$ be its closed convex hull. Around each $p_i$ choose pairwise disjoint round disks $D_i\subset\operatorname{int}(Q_0)$ with no other zero, and inside each choose a small centered closed square $Q_i$. The punctured $D_i$ is zero-free. These filled polygons are explicit convex sets. Their boundary loops are radially homotopic through nonzero values of $(P,Q)$ to the source circle and to $\partial D_i$, respectively: if $r_0(\theta)$ is the radial function of $\partial Q_0$, use $((1-s)r_0(\theta)+s)e^{i\theta}$; if $\rho_i(\theta)$ is the radial function of $\partial Q_i$ about $p_i$ and $R_i$ is the radius of $D_i$, use $p_i+((1-s)\rho_i(\theta)+sR_i)e^{i\theta}$. Thus their degrees agree with the original boundary and local degrees. The domain $A=Q_0\setminus\bigcup_i\operatorname{int}(Q_i)$ contains no zero.

Triangulate $A$ by a finite vertical decomposition. Choose a linear coordinate direction so no boundary edge is vertical and all boundary vertices have distinct first coordinates; there are only finitely many forbidden directions. Between consecutive vertex coordinates, the boundary edges are linear graphs in a fixed vertical order, so the part of $A$ in each open slab is a finite union of trapezoids or triangles. Take closures, omit zero-area pieces, and on each vertical dividing line collect the endpoints from both adjacent slabs and subdivide the cell sides by this finite set. Every resulting cell is a convex polygon; triangulate it by joining one interior point to its boundary vertices. This gives a finite face-to-face triangulation of the explicit polygonal domain, with no use of polygonal Jordan separation, surface classification, or Schoenflies.

For a path $q:[0,1]\to S^1$, continuity gives around each parameter value an interval of radius $2r$ mapping into a proper open arc; the intervals of radius $r$ cover $[0,1]$. A finite subcover and the minimum of its radii give a mesh so every path segment lies in one such arc. Lift the argument successively on the segments and match at endpoints. Its endpoint difference $\Delta(q)$ is independent of the lift, additive under concatenation, and changes sign under reversal. For a homotopy square into $S^1$, take around each point an axis-parallel rectangle with coordinate half-widths $2r,2s$ mapped into a proper arc. The concentric half-size rectangles cover the square; a finite subcover and the minimum $\delta$ of all its half-widths give a rectangular grid with both horizontal and vertical mesh less than $\delta$. Each cell then maps into one proper arc, so its boundary increment is zero. Summing over cells cancels internal edges. For a homotopy through loops the side paths cancel, proving loop-degree invariance. In particular a loop extending over a triangle has total boundary increment zero.

Put $g=(P+iQ)/\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ on $A$. For each oriented triangle of its triangulation, the three edge increments of $g$ sum to zero because $g$ extends over that triangle. Sum over the finite triangulation: each interior edge occurs twice with opposite orientations and cancels. The remaining boundary is the outer polygon positively and the square holes negatively, hence $\deg(g|_{\partial D^2})=\sum_i\deg(g|_{\partial D_i})$ by the radial homotopies. At a nondegenerate zero $p_i$, the derivative of $(P,Q)$ is invertible and its local degree is the sign of its determinant: Taylor's estimate makes the straight homotopy to the invertible linear map nonzero on a sufficiently small circle. In an adapted foliation chart $\omega=a\,dz$, so $\beta=(a\circ h)d(z\circ h)$ and at a zero $D(P,Q)=(a\circ h)\operatorname{Hess}(z\circ h)$; the determinant sign is positive for a definite Hessian (center) and negative for an indefinite Hessian (saddle). Therefore $1=\sum_i\operatorname{ind}_{p_i}(X)=c-s$. If there were no zeros, $g$ would extend over the whole disk and have boundary degree zero, contradicting the computed degree $1$.
